name: Tricuspid valve
func: A three-leaflet one-way door between the right atrium and right ventricle. It lets used, oxygen-poor blood from the body fill the right ventricle and shuts when the ventricle pumps, stopping backflow.

levels.kid:
Blood that has already delivered its oxygen around your body comes back to the right side of your heart. It lands in the top-right room first.

The **tricuspid valve** is the door between that top-right room and the bottom-right room. "Tri" means three, because the door has three flaps, like a three-piece curtain.

When the bottom room is relaxing, the flaps open and blood flows in. When the bottom room squeezes to send blood to the lungs, the three flaps press together and close, so blood can't sneak back up. Little strings hold the flaps so they don't flip inside out.
levels.hs:
The **tricuspid valve** (the **right atrioventricular valve**) lies between the **right atrium** and the **right ventricle**. It has three leaflets: **anterior**, **posterior** and **septal**. It is the largest of the four heart valves and sits at the front-right of the heart, roughly behind the lower half of the sternum, with the mitral valve to its left and slightly behind it.

Like the mitral valve, its leaflets are tethered by **chordae tendineae** to **papillary muscles**, here usually three: anterior, posterior and septal. A muscle bundle called the **moderator band** (septomarginal trabecula) crosses the right ventricle to the anterior papillary muscle and carries part of the heart's electrical wiring.

It opens during **diastole**, letting oxygen-poor blood from the body (via the venae cavae and right atrium) fill the ventricle, and closes in **systole**, helping produce the **first heart sound**. It is heard best at the **lower left sternal border**.

A small amount of leakage (trivial regurgitation) is found in many healthy people on ultrasound and is normal.
levels.college:
The tricuspid annulus is larger and more pliable than the mitral annulus and sits slightly closer to the apex (more apically displaced). This **apical offset of the septal leaflet** is a key echo landmark separating the right from the left AV valve, and an exaggerated offset defines **Ebstein anomaly**.

The septal leaflet attaches along the interventricular septum close to the **membranous septum**. The **AV node** and **bundle of His** lie in the **triangle of Koch**, bounded by the tendon of Todaro, the coronary sinus opening and the septal leaflet's hinge line. Surgeons must avoid sutures in this zone or they can cause complete heart block.

The **right coronary artery** runs in the AV groove around the anterior and posterior parts of the annulus.

Physiology: right-sided pressures are low (RV systolic pressure about 25 mmHg), so tricuspid flow velocities are low. Tricuspid murmurs get **louder with inspiration** (**Carvallo's sign**), because breathing in lowers chest pressure and draws more blood into the right heart. The velocity of a regurgitant jet across the valve is used on echo to **estimate pulmonary artery pressure** (simplified Bernoulli equation: pressure gradient ≈ 4v²).
levels.phd:
Embryologically the AV valves form from the **endocardial cushions**: in the AV canal, endothelial cells undergo **endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT)**, driven by signals such as **BMP2**, **TGF-β**, **Notch** and **NFATc1**, and the resulting mesenchyme is remodeled into leaflets. The tricuspid leaflets also form by **delamination (undermining)** of the inner RV myocardium; failure of this step leaves leaflets stuck to the ventricular wall, the mechanism behind **Ebstein anomaly**, in which the effective valve sits low and part of the RV becomes "atrialized."

Most adult tricuspid regurgitation is **secondary (functional)**: the leaflets are normal, but the annulus dilates and the leaflets are tethered as the RV and right atrium enlarge, usually from left-heart disease or pulmonary hypertension. Annular dilation mostly occurs along the free walls (anterior and posterior), since the septal portion is anchored to the fibrous skeleton. This is why surgical **annuloplasty rings** are often incomplete, sparing the septal segment and the conduction system.

Atrial-type functional TR is increasingly recognized in long-standing **atrial fibrillation**, where right atrial dilation stretches the annulus even with normal RV size.

Primary tricuspid disease is rarer: **carcinoid heart disease** (serotonin-rich secretions from metastatic neuroendocrine tumors cause plaque-like fibrosis that fixes the leaflets; the lungs inactivate much of it before the left heart), **rheumatic disease**, **pacemaker lead** impingement, and endocarditis.
levels.expert:
**Tricuspid regurgitation (TR)** gives a **holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border** that **increases with inspiration**. Severe TR shows **giant "cv" (v) waves** in the jugular venous pulse, a **pulsatile liver**, peripheral edema and ascites. **Tricuspid stenosis** is rare and usually rheumatic, with a diastolic rumble and a prominent **a wave**.

**Right-sided infective endocarditis** typically involves the tricuspid valve, especially with infected intravenous lines, pacemaker leads or injection-related infections. Its emboli go to the **lungs** (septic pulmonary emboli seen as multiple cavitating nodules on CT), not the brain, unless there is a **patent foramen ovale** allowing paradoxical embolism.

**Ebstein anomaly** presents with cyanosis, an enlarged right atrium, right bundle branch block and often an accessory pathway (**WPW**).

Imaging: transthoracic echo shows leaflet anatomy and the regurgitant jet; the peak jet velocity estimates RV systolic pressure. Cardiac MRI quantifies RV size and function, which drive timing of intervention.

Treatment in general terms: treat the cause (left-heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, AF), diuretics for congestion, surgical **annuloplasty or repair** usually done at the time of left-sided valve surgery, valve replacement when repair fails, and a growing range of **transcatheter repair and replacement** devices. Endocarditis is treated with prolonged antibiotics and sometimes surgery.

keyPoints: Between right atrium and right ventricle; three leaflets
Largest heart valve; sits slightly more apical than the mitral
AV node lies near the septal leaflet (triangle of Koch)
Right-sided endocarditis sends emboli to the lungs

test.q: The tricuspid valve separates which two chambers?
A tricuspid regurgitation murmur gets louder with:
test.explain: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart (Carvallo's sign).

test.q: A congenital disorder where the tricuspid leaflets are displaced toward the apex is ______ anomaly.
test.explain: Failed delamination leaves leaflets stuck to the RV wall, 'atrializing' part of the ventricle.

test.q: Septic emboli from tricuspid endocarditis usually lodge in the:
test.explain: Blood from the right heart goes to the lungs, so right-sided vegetations embolize to the pulmonary arteries.

test.q: Name the conduction structure surgeons must avoid near the septal leaflet.
test.explain: The AV node and bundle of His sit in the triangle of Koch; injury causes heart block.
